  "text": "When the reservoir emptied, our old house appeared with its upstairs windows open.

My brother said not to go.

“The mud will take your boots.”

He had been practical since we were children. I borrowed his boots.

The village lay half a mile beyond the warning signs. Roofs had folded inward. The church clock showed twenty past four, though I remembered it stopping long before the flood.

Our house still had its blue door.

Inside, everything stood lower than it should. The table had sunk to its knees. Silt filled the fireplace. A fish skeleton rested where we used to leave the post.

I went looking for the marks beside the kitchen doorway.

Mum measured us every birthday, pressing a cereal box flat against our heads. My brother always stretched. She always pretended not to notice.

The pencil had washed away.

I scraped the doorframe with my thumbnail until a pale strip emerged, bare of everything.

Outside, my brother called my name.

He stood in the doorway wearing office shoes, already ruined.

“Find anything?”

I shook my head.

He looked at the strip of wood. Then he turned his back to it and stood straight.

“Go on.”

“We haven’t got a pencil.”

He took his keys from his pocket.

I held one above his head and scratched a short line. Then he made mine.

We left before the rain started.

At the car, he opened the boot for our muddy shoes. I had to lean on him to pull his boots off. He complained that I was stretching the leather, and drove me home in his socks."
